summary:
New South Wales sets its own discrimination, document, facilities and custody rules inside Australia's national framework; federal law, passports and marriage are carried by the national record. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 has covered transgender status since 1996 and prohibits discrimination in work, public education, goods and services, banking, health care, property and nightclubs. Section 16 of the Mental Health Act 2007 states that sexual orientation and gender identity are not mental illnesses.

Birth certificates and driver licences are issued by the state, while passports and marriage are Commonwealth matters. Since 1 July 2025 a change of sex on a New South Wales birth certificate no longer requires surgery: the applicant files a form, supplies a good-faith witness who is an unrelated adult known for at least a year, and pays a $73 fee. The replacement certificate does not disclose that the record was changed.

The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 took effect on 4 April 2025. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm carry up to five years' imprisonment, and taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years. Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from that date and refer matters into civil pathways. The bill passed unamended on 22 March 2024 by 22 votes to 4 in the upper house, with limited religious and parental exemptions that include sermons preaching against homosexuality.

Fatal violence against a trans visitor is on record. Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines visiting Australia, was killed in Wagga Wagga; the perpetrator pleaded guilty to manslaughter and received a 22-month term.

Hate-crime law is narrower than the discrimination statute. The Crimes Amendment (Publicly Threatening and Inciting Violence) Act 2018, passed unanimously by both houses in June 2018, repealed the earlier vilification provisions and created a criminal offence effective 13 August 2018 carrying up to three years' imprisonment; the grounds covered remain limited to sexual orientation, so gender identity sits outside New South Wales vilification law. Nazi symbols were banned under the Crimes Act 1900 by unanimous vote, assented on 19 August 2022 and effective immediately, with the LGBTIQ community named among those the provision protects.

Exemptions in the Anti-Discrimination Act permit discrimination on grounds of sex, gender, pregnancy and homosexuality in sport and in non-public religious schools. Transgender people can be excluded from female sports categories on that basis, and religiously run adoption agencies may refuse same-sex couples.

Facilities are covered at local government level rather than by state statute: Sydney City Council adopted a gender-neutral bathrooms policy in April 2023.
tangentialFactors:
A judicial inquiry announced in November 2021 began work in November 2022 into LGBTIQ hate crimes, examining 88 deaths of gay men between 1970 and 2000; New South Wales Police were called to give evidence in December 2022. The remit as reported concerns homophobic killings rather than violence against transgender people.

In October 2020 the lower house passed a unanimous non-binding bipartisan motion calling for human rights, dignity and respect for transgender individuals. It carries no legal effect.

A government hate crimes bill introduced in March 2026 concerns violence against gay and bisexual men, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment, and had not been debated in either house at the time of the source.
localsOnly:
Until 30 June 2025 a change of sex on a New South Wales birth certificate required sexual reassignment surgery and a $153 fee. The divorce requirement was abolished in June 2018, and 766 sex changes had been recorded by September 2025. The number of changes is not capped, unlike name changes, which are limited to once every 12 months and three per lifetime.

The High Court of Australia ruled in April 2014, in a case originating in New South Wales, that the law permits registration of a change of sex to non-specific, and since March 2022 rainbow birth certificates without sex or gender listed have been available to people born or adopted in the state.

Since 1996 New South Wales prisoner protocols and guidelines allow transgender people who have had sexual reassignment surgery to be housed in female prisons for protection. An undisclosed New South Wales government settlement was granted in November 2024 to a transgender person held in a male prison.

Inner West Council in Sydney voted to approve transgender health leave for its staff; the measure has not taken effect because it requires the local government minister's signature.
outOfScopeNotes:
The text of the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024 could not be retrieved, so its specific provisions are not detailed here.

Commencement of the Inner West Council transgender health leave remains unresolved pending ministerial signature.

No New South Wales-specific data was located on screening or entry treatment of trans travellers; those processes are national and are carried by the national record. No sourced state-level figures on trans-targeted violence were located, and the Bruno case is a single documented killing rather than a rate.
